steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Probabilistic inference problems show up all over AI, and algorithmically they are tackled by casting them as problems like model counting. In this work we want to approach inference questions for higher-order objects, specifically Skolem functions: we want to compute the number of possible Skolem functions for a given specification F(X,Y). Counting Skolem functions is the natural analog of #SAT for Skolem functions. It has been explored recently in the context of counting level-2 solutions for valid Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBFs).

To be more precise, recall that given two sets X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} and Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{m}\} of variables and a Boolean formula F(X,Y) over X\cup Y, the problem of Boolean functional synthesis is to compute a vector \Psi=\langle\psi_{1},\dots,\psi_{m}\rangle of Boolean functions \psi_{i}, which are often called Skolem functions, such that \exists YF(X,Y)\equiv F(X,\Psi(X)). Informally, we are given a specification between inputs and outputs, and the task is to synthesize a function vector \Psi that maps each assignment of the inputs to an assignment of the outputs so that the combined assignment meets the specification (whenever such an assignment exists). Skolem synthesis is a fundamental problem in formal methods, and both theoreticians and practitioners have studied it over the past few decades. In the past few years techniques have been developed that show promise of scalability, since they can handle challenging specifications.

Today's Skolem synthesis engines are scalable in a way that is reminiscent of SAT solvers in the early 2000s. Because SAT solvers became scalable, researchers looked for algorithmic frameworks for problems beyond satisfiability, like MaxSAT, model counting, sampling, and so on. Developing scalable techniques for these problems also helped bring in new applications, even though many of them were not envisioned when the investigation started. In a similar way, and partly motivated by the development of scalable techniques for functional synthesis, we study the Skolem counting problem. In Section 1.2 we observe that algorithms for these tasks also have potential applications in security and in engineering specifications. Since it is a natural problem, our study also leads to deep technical connections between counting functions and counting propositional models, and to new techniques, which is of independent interest.

Counting Skolem functions does raise new technical challenges. The existing techniques for propositional model counting either build (implicitly or explicitly) a representation of the space of all models or at least enumerate a small number of models, which in practice means a few tens to hundreds of models of formulas constrained by random XORs. These approaches are unlikely to work efficiently for Skolem function counting, where even finding one Skolem function is hard.

## 1.1 Technical Contribution

The main contribution of this work is a new algorithmic framework called \mathsf{SkolemFC}. It approximates the Skolem function count with a theoretical guarantee, and it only uses linearly many calls to an approximate model counter and almost-uniform sampler. First, we observe that Skolem function counting can be reduced to an exponential number of model counting calls, and this serves as a baseline Skolem function counter. The core technical idea of \mathsf{SkolemFC} is to reduce approximate Skolem function counting to only linearly many (in m=|Y|) calls to propositional model counters. In particular, \mathsf{SkolemFC} can approximate the number of Skolem functions without enumerating even one Skolem function. Approximate model counting and almost-uniform sampling can be done with logarithmically many calls to a \mathsf{SAT} oracle, so we show that Skolem function counting can also be reduced to polynomially many calls to a \mathsf{SAT} oracle.

To measure the impact of the algorithm we implement \mathsf{SkolemFC} and show its potential on a set of benchmarks from prior studies on Skolem function synthesis. Out of 609 instances, \mathsf{SkolemFC} solved 375 instances, while a baseline solver solved only eight instances. For context, the state-of-the-art Skolem function synthesis tool \mathsf{Manthan} \mathsf{2} handled 509 instances from these benchmarks, and its precursor \mathsf{Manthan} managed only 356 instances, with a timeout of 7200 seconds.

## 1.2 Applications
- specification synthesis (constructing F(X,Y)) + function synthesis iterate; many Skolem functions -> vague spec, needs strengthening; log count suffices
- security/reliability: diverse functionally equivalent implementations; whether spec admits diverse functions (may be unique) -> counting needed, rough estimate; primitive for the approach
- SMT counting: uninterpreted functions; Skolem functions restricted but large class (depend on all X variables)
- incremental evaluation via reducing sampling to counting; random XOR constraints; approximately uniform function conditioned on previous answers

## 1.3 Organization
- Section 2 related work, Section 3 preliminaries, Section 4 main contribution, Section 5 experiments, Section 6 conclusion

## 1.2 Applications

There are several potential application areas where this problem comes up.

The first and main motivation comes from the observation that specification synthesis (i.e., the process of constructing F(X,Y)) and function synthesis are part of an iterative process, where one modifies specifications iteratively based on the functions that the underlying engine builds. Here a helpful measure is the number of possible semantically different functions that satisfy the specification, because a large number of possible Skolem functions often means the specification is vague and needs to be strengthened. The count is used qualitatively here, so an approximate order of magnitude (log count) is enough.

In system security and reliability, a classic technique is to generate and use a diverse variety of functionally equivalent implementations of components. Classically this is done with code transformations that preserve the function computed, but we may also want to produce a variety of functions that satisfy a common specification. Unlike with code transformations, it is not immediately clear whether a specification even admits a diverse collection of functions – the function may in fact be uniquely defined. So counting such functions is needed to assess whether this approach is worth taking, and again a rough order of magnitude estimate is enough. Approximate counting of the functions could also be a useful primitive for realizing this approach.

A major challenge in designing counting techniques for SMT is handling uninterpreted functions. Skolem functions capture a restricted but large enough class of uninterpreted functions (namely, the case where a given uninterpreted function is allowed to depend on all X variables), so progress in Skolem function counting is needed if we want progress on the general problem of counting uninterpreted functions in SMT.

Concretely, given a query input, we can estimate the number of functions that produce each output: this is trivial if the range is small (e.g., Boolean), and otherwise we can add random XOR constraints to specify the output incrementally. Once an output is specified for the query point, we can keep these constraints when estimating the number of consistent functions for later queries, and in this way we get an approximately uniform function conditioned on the answers to the previous queries.

## 1.3 Organization

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section 2 discusses related work and Section 3 presents notation and preliminaries. Section 4 presents the main technical contribution of our work. Section 5 presents the empirical analysis of the prototype implementation of \mathsf{SkolemFC}. Section 6 concludes.

steps.text:
Probabilistic inference problems arise throughout AI and are tackled algorithmically by casting them as problems such as model counting [1,2]. In this work, we are interested in inference questions for higher-order objects, specifically Skolem functions: we wish to compute the number of possible Skolem functions for a given specification F(X,Y). Counting Skolem functions is the natural analog of #SAT for Skolem functions, and has recently been explored in the context of counting level-2 solutions for valid Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBFs) [3].

More precisely, recall that given two sets X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} and Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{m}\} of variables and a Boolean formula F(X,Y) over X\cup Y, the problem of Boolean functional synthesis is to compute a vector \Psi=\langle\psi_{1},\dots,\psi_{m}\rangle of Boolean functions \psi_{i}, often called Skolem functions, such that \exists YF(X,Y)\equiv F(X,\Psi(X)). Informally, given a specification between inputs and outputs, the task is to synthesize a function vector \Psi that maps each assignment of the inputs to an assignment of the outputs so that the combined assignment meets the specification (whenever such an assignment exists). Skolem synthesis is a fundamental problem in formal methods and has been investigated by theoreticians and practitioners alike over the past few decades. The past few years have seen the development of techniques that show promise of scalability in handling challenging specifications [4,5,6,7,8].

The scalability of today’s Skolem synthesis engines is reminiscent of that of SAT solvers in the early 2000s. Motivated by the scalability of SAT solvers [9], researchers sought algorithmic frameworks for problems beyond satisfiability, such as MaxSAT [10,11], model counting [1,2], sampling [12], and the like. The development of scalable techniques for these problems also helped usher in new applications, many of which the initial investigation had not envisioned. In a similar vein, motivated in part by the development of scalable techniques for functional synthesis, we investigate the Skolem counting problem. In Section 1.2 we observe that algorithms for such tasks also have potential applications in security and the engineering of specifications. As it is a natural problem, our study also leads to deep technical connections between counting functions and counting propositional models, and to the development of new techniques, which is of independent interest.

Counting Skolem functions indeed raises new technical challenges. Existing techniques for propositional model counting either construct (implicitly or explicitly) a representation of the space of all models [13,14,15] or at least enumerate a small number of models [16,17,18,19], which in practice amounts to a few tens to hundreds of models of formulas constrained by random XORs. Such approaches are unlikely to work efficiently for Skolem function counting, where even finding one Skolem function is hard.

## 1.1 Technical Contribution

The primary contribution of this work is a novel algorithmic framework, called \mathsf{SkolemFC}, that approximates the Skolem function count with a theoretical guarantee using only linearly many calls to an approximate model counter and almost-uniform sampler. First, we observe that Skolem function counting can be reduced to an exponential number of model counting calls, which serves as a baseline Skolem function counter. The core technical idea of \mathsf{SkolemFC} is to reduce approximate Skolem function counting to only linearly many (in m=|Y|) calls to propositional model counters. Of particular note, \mathsf{SkolemFC} can approximate the number of Skolem functions without enumerating even one Skolem function. As approximate model counting and almost-uniform sampling can be done with logarithmically many calls to a \mathsf{SAT} oracle, we show that Skolem function counting can also be reduced to polynomially many calls to a \mathsf{SAT} oracle.

To measure the impact of the algorithm, we implement \mathsf{SkolemFC} and demonstrate its potential on a set of benchmarks arising from prior studies of Skolem function synthesis. Out of 609 instances, \mathsf{SkolemFC} solved 375, while a baseline solver solved only eight. For context, the state-of-the-art Skolem function synthesis tool \mathsf{Manthan} \mathsf{2} [8] tackled 509 instances from these benchmarks, while its precursor, \mathsf{Manthan} [20], managed only 356, with a timeout of 7200 seconds.

## 1.2 Applications

This problem arises in several potential application areas.

The first and primary motivation stems from the observation that specification synthesis [21,22] (i.e., the process of constructing F(X,Y)) and function synthesis form part of an iterative process in which one modifies specifications based on the functions constructed by the underlying engine. Here, a helpful measure is the number of possible semantically different functions that satisfy the specification, since a large number of possible Skolem functions often indicates that the specification is vague and needs strengthening. The count is used qualitatively here, so an approximate order of magnitude (log count) suffices.

In system security and reliability, a classic technique is to generate and use a diverse variety of functionally equivalent implementations of components [23]. While this is classically achieved by code transformations that preserve the function computed, we may also be interested in producing a variety of functions that satisfy a common specification. Unlike with code transformations, it is not immediately clear whether a specification even admits a diverse collection of functions – the function may in fact be uniquely defined. Counting such functions is therefore necessary to assess the potential value of this approach, and again a rough order of magnitude estimate suffices. Approximate counting of the functions may also be a useful primitive for realizing such an approach.

A major challenge in designing counting techniques for SMT [24,25] lies in handling uninterpreted functions [26]. Since Skolem functions capture a restricted but large enough class of uninterpreted functions (namely, the case where a given uninterpreted function may depend on all X variables), progress in Skolem function counting is needed if we hope to make progress on the general problem of counting uninterpreted functions in SMT.

Although synthesis of Skolem functions remains challenging in general, approximate counting enables a kind of incremental evaluation using the standard techniques for reducing sampling to counting. Concretely, given a query input, we can estimate the number of functions that produce each output: this is trivial if the range is small (e.g., Boolean), and otherwise we can introduce random XOR constraints to specify the output incrementally. Once an output is specified for the query point, we may retain these constraints when estimating the number of consistent functions for subsequent queries, thereby obtaining an approximately uniform function conditioned on the answers to previous queries.

## 1.3 Organization

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we discuss related work in Section 2 and present notation and preliminaries in Section 3. Section 4 presents the primary technical contribution of our work, and Section 5 presents the empirical analysis of the prototype implementation of \mathsf{SkolemFC}. We conclude in Section 6.
